item.title: Reverse game theory could keep AI agents in check
item.description: On November 3, MIT Technology Review described reverse game theory as designing the rules so following them becomes the rational move for an AI agent. A preprint by MIT economist Stephen Morris proposes rewarding a model for how well its answers predict a second model's, making deliberately underperforming on a test a losing bet.

item.title: Word of the Day: zugzwang — Daily Learning
item.description: Zugzwang (TSOOK-tsvahng) is a noun from German Zug, move, and Zwang, compulsion, naming a chess position where you must move but every legal move worsens your position. In the negotiation, she was in zugzwang: conceding on price would cost her margin, walking away would cost her the client, and stalling would cost her trust.
item.content:encoded: Zugzwang (TSOOK-tsvahng) is a noun from German Zug, move, and Zwang, compulsion, naming a chess position where you must move but every legal move worsens your position. In the negotiation, she was in zugzwang: conceding on price would cost her margin, walking away would cost her the client, and stalling would cost her trust.

item.description: When the host, who knows where the car is, opens a door to reveal a goat, switching doubles your chance of winning from 1/3 to 2/3. Your first pick was probably wrong, so that 2/3 now rests on the one door still closed.

item.title: Statistics: Benford's Law — Daily Learning
item.description: In many real-world datasets, 1 is the leading digit about 30% of the time and 9 only about 5%, far from the roughly 11% each you would expect if digits were random. That uneven falloff is a tripwire for made-up numbers.

item.title: Big Idea: The Sleeping Beauty Problem — Daily Learning
item.description: On Sunday Beauty is put to sleep, and a fair coin decides whether she wakes on Monday only or on Monday and Tuesday with her memory erased, so she never knows which day it is or whether she has woken before. The Sleeping Beauty problem still splits Bayesians between 1/2 and 1/3, over what counts as evidence when you are the one being sampled.

item.title: Word of the Day: aporia — Daily Learning
item.description: Aporia (uh-POR-ee-uh) is a noun from Greek a-poros, literally “no way through,” for the genuine puzzlement when two equally strong arguments collide and force you to rethink the question itself. “After an hour of debate, the team hit an aporia: every fix for the bug introduced a worse one, and nobody could say which trade-off was right.”

item.title: Statistics: Overfitting and the Bias–Variance Tradeoff — Daily Learning
item.description: Say a betting model tuned to every quirk of the last 100 games looks unbeatable on those games, yet predicts the next 20 worse than a simpler model. That gap is the bias–variance tradeoff, the balance between a model too stiff to catch real patterns and one too jumpy to ignore noise, judged on unseen data rather than zero error on the past.

item.title: Big Idea: Braess's Paradox — Daily Learning
item.description: Adding a road can make everyone's trip slower, because each driver picks the route that looks fastest for them alone. In the traffic-network example, a zero-time connector pulls everyone onto one route, and the trip becomes 80 minutes for everyone.
